readerTitle: Two near-misses at a dental clinic: which fix fits which mistake?
caseNote: 가상 사례 (동네 치과, 회사 IT팀 신규 입사자 계정 발급) + 실제 관찰 (의료기관의 환자 확인 방식)
insight: 실수마다 맞는 도구가 다르다. 손이나 시스템이 미끄러지는 실수는 구조로 막고(실수 방지), 사람의 판단과 대화가 필요한 단계는 짧은 체크리스트로 지킨다.
misconception: 품질 문제가 생기면 직원에게 '더 조심하라'고 하거나 체크리스트 항목을 하나 더 넣으면 해결된다.

sources.text: The Joint Commission, National Patient Safety Goals (환자 확인 시 두 가지 이상의 식별 정보 사용)
치과와 IT팀 사례는 설명용 가상 예시

factChecks.note: "많은 병원이 이름과 생년월일 등 두 가지 식별 정보로 환자를 확인한다"는 내용은 The Joint Commission의 National Patient Safety Goals(NPSG.01.01.01)에 근거합니다. 게시 전 최신 버전의 항목 번호와 문구를 다시 확인하세요.
치과 사례(같은 이름의 환자, 복약 질문 누락)와 IT팀 사례는 모두 가상입니다. 수치나 실제 사고 통계는 쓰지 않았습니다. 의료 조언으로 읽히지 않도록 운영 관점에서만 서술했는지 검토하세요.
OPS-06-09(수술 안전 체크리스트 사례)와 겹치지 않도록 수술 체크리스트 연구는 언급하지 않았습니다.

cards.title: Two near-misses at a dental clinic
body: Dr. Lee runs a busy six-chair dental clinic. Last month, nothing went wrong. But twice, something almost did.
Once, a hygienist nearly worked from the wrong patient's X-rays. Another time, nobody asked a patient about a new medication before treatment. Two problems. Should they get the same fix?

image.label: Dental clinic front desk with two patient folders side by side
image.brief: 따뜻한 일러스트 스타일. 작은 치과 접수대 위에 이름이 거의 같은 환자 파일 두 개가 나란히 놓여 있고, 뒤로 진료 의자가 보임. 실제 병원·브랜드 로고 없음. 위험이 아닌 '아슬아슬한 순간' 느낌.

cards.title: Two patients, nearly the same name.
body: Two patients are both named J. Park. Staff open charts by typing a name and clicking the first match. On a rushed morning, the hygienist opened the wrong one.

options.text: Remind everyone at the team meeting to be more careful
options.feedback: Cheap and quick, but attention fades by the next rush. A fix that depends on people never slipping isn't a fix.

options.text: Add "confirm the patient's name" to the morning checklist
options.feedback: A **checklist** helps, but the name is exactly what's confusing here. And a checked box can't stop a wrong click.

options.text: Make the system open a chart only after staff enter the date of birth too
options.feedback: This is **mistake-proofing**: the wrong action becomes hard to do at all. Two J. Parks rarely share a birthday.

cards.title: Block the slip, don't just warn about it.
body: The X-ray mix-up was a slip: a fast click by someone who knew better. Slips don't respond well to reminders, because nobody chooses to make them.
**Mistake-proofing** changes the setup so the error can't easily happen. Many hospitals already require two identifiers, such as name and date of birth, before acting on a patient record.
Dr. Lee's fix costs one extra field. It works on the tired morning and the calm afternoon alike.

cards.title: The question that gets skipped.
body: Before treatment, someone should ask: any new medications, allergies or health changes? On calm days, staff ask. On busy days, it sometimes slips because everyone assumes someone else asked.

options.text: A check-in tablet that won't let patients continue until they tick "no changes"
options.feedback: It blocks skipping, but a patient can tap through without thinking. This step needs a real conversation, which a blocked screen can't force.

options.text: A four-line checklist the assistant reads aloud at the chair before every treatment
options.feedback: A short **checklist** fits steps that need human judgment and get skipped under pressure. Reading it aloud also makes clear who asked.

options.text: Hire another receptionist so the front desk is less rushed
options.feedback: Less pressure helps, but it costs a salary and still leaves the question to memory. Busy days will come back.

cards.title: Match the fix to the mistake.
body: The two near-misses looked alike. They weren't. One was a slip of the hand. The other was a skipped conversation.

breakdown.label: Mistake-proofing
breakdown.detail: Fast, automatic errors. Make the wrong action hard or impossible.

breakdown.label: Checklist
breakdown.detail: Steps needing judgment that get dropped under pressure. Make them visible and owned.

cards.callout: Ask first: did someone slip, or did someone skip?
cards.softwareNote: Software teams face the same split. Required fields and blocked deploys stop slips. A short release checklist covers steps that need a person to look and decide.

cards.title: Both tools can quietly break.
body: Checklists grow. Each incident adds a line, and soon a 4-item list is 20 items that people tick without reading. Keep it short, and remove lines when you add them.
Mistake-proofs invite workarounds. If entering a birth date feels slow, someone tapes the common ones to the monitor. When staff bypass a safeguard, treat it as a design problem and ask why.

cards.title: Now it's an IT team inside a company.
body: Your IT team sets up accounts for new hires. To save time, they copy access from a colleague in a similar job. Twice this quarter, a new hire got access to payroll files they shouldn't see.

options.text: Add "double-check permissions" to the setup checklist
options.feedback: Better than nothing, but copying is a fast slip, and long permission lists are hard to eyeball. A **checklist** catches some of it.

options.text: Replace copying with set access packages per role, with extra access needing a manager's approval
options.feedback: This is **mistake-proofing**. The risky shortcut disappears, and the safe path becomes the easy one.

options.text: Run a full access review once a month
options.feedback: Reviews find problems, but only after someone has had the wrong access for weeks. It catches mistakes instead of preventing them.

cards.softwareNote: The same thinking applies to user roles in your own product: default roles prevent the slip of handing every new user admin rights.

cards.title: Slips need a block. Skips need a checklist.
body: This lesson used two ideas from this unit: **mistake-proofing** for errors people make without choosing to, and **checklists** for steps that need judgment but get dropped when busy.
**Try it today:** list your last three near-misses. Mark each as a slip or a skip, and pick one fix that matches.
